problem: DRL mapless goal-driven navigation methods (goal-conditional learning) encode the scene with a goal-agnostic encoder (e.g., ConvNet) and only concatenate the physical goal (polar coordinates) to the latent features afterwards. The resulting representation keeps goal-irrelevant features that hurt RL data efficiency. No prior work used a ViT-enabled DRL policy for UGV goal-driven mapless navigation.
motivation: Map-based SLAM navigation depends on map precision and breaks down in unknown environments, which makes end-to-end mapless visual navigation attractive. However, DRL in this setting is notoriously data-inefficient. The authors observe that when the goal is decoupled from perception, the encoder must represent the whole scene, and parts of that representation act 'adversarially' during RL. Feeding the goal into the scene encoder should instead let attention focus on goal-relevant regions.
key_idea: Treat the goal (normalized distance and heading error) as an input token, not a downstream condition. A BERT-style goal token is prepended to the fisheye-image patch tokens of a small ViT variant (Goal-guided Transformer, GoT). GoT is pre-trained by imitating human demonstrations, and a SAC policy is then trained on top of GoT's goal-oriented representation.
insight: Fusing the goal at the input of self-attention yields sparser, goal-directed attention. Against goal-conditional ViT-SAC, the Gini coefficient is higher (0.927/0.848/0.901 vs 0.802/0.616/0.695) and the Shannon-Wiener index is lower (0.896/1.133/0.984 vs 1.613/1.807/1.545) on three episodes. Attention-flow maps show a 'visual path' bending toward the goal even when another turn is feasible. The learned attention is causally important: perturbing high-weight attention (>0.995) to 10% or to a moving average clearly lowers success rate. Both GoT-SAC variants (with and without expert-prior pretraining) converge faster and higher than ViT-SAC (training efficiency +129% and +86%) at nearly identical cost (36.9 vs 36.2 MFLOPs, 0.46 vs 0.45M params), so the gain comes from where the goal enters, not from capacity.
method: Goal token: a 2-D goal state (normalized relative distance min(||p-q||/λ,1) and heading error normalized to [-1,1]) is mapped by an MLP to a D-dim token. It is fixed at the first position (like BERT's special token) and added to the position embeddings.

Goal-guided Transformer (GoT): a ViT variant taking the goal token plus 8x8 patches of 4 stacked 160x120 fisheye RGB frames (220° FOV, Gaussian pixel-noise augmented). It has 2 encoder blocks with 4 heads each (MSA, LN, MLP, FC, residuals) and outputs latent h = GoT(s, G).

Expert-prior pretraining (DIL): GoT plus an action head is behavior-cloned on human teleop demos (Logitech G29 wheel/pedals, 2 licensed drivers). The data are 200 trajectories / 17,215 pairs, split 8:2 into train/val, with early stopping on validation loss. The best model initializes RL (hot start).

GoT-SAC: a soft actor-critic with double Q-networks, target network and automatic entropy temperature, acting on the GoT latent h. It outputs continuous [v ∈ [0,1], ω ∈ [-π/2, π/2]] sent to the UGV via ROS.

Reward shaping: the total reward is r = r_h + r_a + r_g + r_c. r_h is progress toward the goal (η_h × distance reduction). r_a = v − η_a|ω| penalizes steering. r_g = +100 within margin ξ of the goal, and r_c = −100 on collision.

Training/transfer: 500 episodes × ≤200 steps in a Gazebo lab replica, with randomized start and goal plus noise augmentation for sim-to-real. At deployment on a SCOUT MINI (Jetson Xavier), goal information comes from VINS-Fusion VSLAM ego-pose.

setting.backbone: Goal-guided Transformer (2-block, 4-head ViT variant) + SAC actor-critic MLPs, trained from scratch (IL pretraining then RL)
setting.training_data: 200 human teleoperated demonstration trajectories (17,215 state-action pairs; reported split 13,372 train / 3,443 val) collected in the Gazebo lab environment for DIL pretraining. RL then runs 500 episodes (max 200 steps each) in Gazebo with randomized start/goal and Gaussian pixel noise.
setting.observation: 4 stacked 160x120 fisheye RGB frames (220° FOV) + 2-D goal state (normalized relative distance, heading error) from odometry; laser used in simulation only for collision detection
setting.action_space: continuous linear velocity v∈[0,1] and angular velocity ω∈[-π/2, π/2]
setting.privileged: Goal-relative distance/heading computed from ground-truth odometry in simulation. In the real world, ego-pose comes from VINS-Fusion VSLAM (~0.1 m ATE). No map is used.

numbers.bench: other:Real-world loop navigation (NTU Robotics Research Center, 4 goals)
numbers.extra: Sim-to-real on SCOUT MINI; ego-pose from VINS-Fusion VSLAM; best model selected per algorithm; success = goal reached within one minute; human engagement if collision likely
numbers.evidence: Table 'Quantitative performance of proposed algorithm compared with baselines' (GoT-SAC rows 1st–4th goal position). AvgDist_goal4 is printed as 6.360.

numbers_note: Simulation success rates (evaluated over 20 seeds × 50 episodes), learning curves, the perturbation study and the head/block ablation are given only as figures (boxplots and curves), so no exact SR numbers exist for simulation. The text only states '+129% and 86%' training efficiency vs ViT-SAC. It also says attention perturbation to 10% makes performance 'degrade catastrophically (62.5%)', and it is unclear whether this is the SR or the drop. Other tables report attention statistics (Gini/Shannon-Wiener) and compute cost (GoT-SAC 36.9 MFLOPs, 0.46M params, 0.24 ms inference, 3.16 hr training). The real-world variance columns (e.g., ±0.049 m, ±0.282 s for goal 1) are omitted from metrics. The unseen office test (5 goals, all reached without collision or engagement) has no table. The demo split numbers in the paper (13,372 + 3,443) do not sum to the stated 17,215.
results: In Gazebo, both GoT-SAC variants (IL-pretrained and from scratch) reach higher reward with lower variance over 5 seeds than ConvNet-SAC and ViT-SAC, with training efficiency improved by over 129% and 86% relative to ViT-SAC. Simulation success-rate boxplots also show GoT-SAC dominating. In a real-world 4-goal loop, GoT-SAC reaches all goals at 100% SR with zero human engagements and the lowest time on goals 2–3 (e.g., 11.987 s vs ViT-SAC 15.432 s). ConvNet-SAC needs 15 engagements, MultiModal CIL drops to 60%/20% SR on goals 2/3, and MoveBase (local map only) needs 10 engagements. GoT-SAC also reached all 5 goals in an unseen office environment without engagement.
limitations: Evaluation is small-scale and non-standard: a single Gazebo lab environment, simulation SR reported only in plots, and a handful of real-world goals with an unspecified trial count, so it is not comparable to standard PointNav benchmarks.
Relies on accurate goal-relative pose (odometry in simulation, VINS-Fusion VSLAM in the real world); the authors note position errors hurt and plan re-localization.
Fails under strong lighting and ground reflections and with unseen dynamic obstacles such as pedestrians dressed similar to the floor; only tested indoors.
builds_on: Behavior cloning / deep imitation learning pretraining
